newsitem.title: UK: "Bad" news for emerging debt markets brings relief.
newsitem.headline: "Bad" news for emerging debt markets brings relief.

text.p: A plunge in emerging debt prices, triggered by fears of higher U.S. interest rates, is probably good for the market and far from marks the end of the road for one of the world's fastest rising assets, fund managers and analysts said on Tuesday.

"I'm glad it's selling off. Otherwise the market keeps going up and it becomes unsustainable...Though we recognise we're losing money for the moment, in the long-run it's more healthy," said Michael Mabbutt, emerging market fixed income fund manager at LGT Assett Management.
"You shake out the recent joiners who thought this was a one-way bet and who can be dangerous for a market," he added.
Emerging debt prices rose by about a third on average last year and showed no signs of stopping in the first two months of 1997.
Then U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan last week jolted investors by, what many took to be, implying that U.S. interest rates would rise soon.
His comments slashed four percent off the market in three days and spreads over U.S. Treasuries for Brady bonds ballooned 75 basis points to an average 470 by Monday's close of trading.
Some traders said Greenspan's comments were as much as anything an excuse to sell, and cash in some profits.
"It doesn't mean the emerging debt market is dead until the Fed eases again. There is enough interest in the market for interest to continue to pick up," said James Edwards, a fund manager
